newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - Payrolls suggests no Fed move in Nov.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Payrolls suggests no Fed move in Nov.

text.p: A surprise decline in U.S. payroll employment in September suggests the Federal Reserve will refrain from raising interest rates at least until December, economists said in a Reuters survey on Friday.
Six of 21 experts projected a possible interest rate hike at the November 13 Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting, down from more than half of 32 polled on Monday.

On Friday morning, the Commerce Department said U.S. non-farm payrolls declined 40,000 in September after rising a revised 241,000 in August. Wall Street economists had expected an increase of about 150,000 to 180,000.
"We expect the Fed to tighten but not just yet, with the payrolls down," said Astrid Adolfson, senior economist at MCM MoneyWatch Inc.

Although the payrolls component of the employment report cheered the credit markets, many experts cautioned that other components were not so market-friendly. More monetary restraint can be expected by year-end, 13 respondents said.

"When you take away this payrolls number, which probably will be revised higher, the other numbers (in the jobs report) are very strong," said Lee Youngdahl, vice president and economist at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co Inc.

The report showed average hourly earnings rose 0.5 percent to $11.92 last month, while the average workweek grew to 34.7 hours from 34.5 hours in August. Economists in a Reuters poll last week forecast a 0.2 percent gain in wages and a 34.5-hour average workweek.
In the wake of the data, Youngdahl said, he "couldn't rule out" a December tighteninng, but it was "a coin toss."

Experts who projected a November tightening said the central bank would be unable to overlook the wage and hours components of Friday's report, and most said they expected more bad news for bonds in the upcoming October jobs data.
"The wage pressures we are continuing to see will stem the enthusiasm" initially shown in the bond market, said Kevin Flanagan, vice president and economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
Five respondents projected no rate change for the foreseeable future.
"The economy is just slowing down enough that (inflation) is not going to be a problem," said Raphael Marrone, a senior analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, who called for no move in November.
